A current Immigration Status Document containing a photograph issued by the Home Office to the holder with a valid endorsement indicating that the named individual may stay in the UK and is allowed to do the type of work in question, together with an official document giving the individual’s permanent National Insurance number and their name issued by a government agency or a previous employer.

List B Group 2: Documents which establish a time-limited statutory excuse for six months

(a follow-up check will be required for an employer to maintain their statutory excuse)

1. A document issued by the Home Office showing that the holder has made an application for leave to enter or remain under Appendix EU to the Immigration Rules (known as the EU Settlement Scheme or EUSS) on or before 30 June 2021 together with a Positive Verification Notice from the Employer Checking Service.

2. A Certificate of Application (non-digital) issued by the Home Office showing that the holder has made an application for leave to enter or remain under Appendix EU to the Immigration Rules (Known as the EU Settlement Scheme or EUSS) on or after 1 July 2021, together with a Positive Verification Notice from the Employer Checking Service.

3. A document issued by the Bailiwick of Jersey, the Bailiwick of Guernsey or the Isle of Man, which has been verified as valid by the Employer Checking Service, showing that the holder has been granted limited leave to enter or remain under Appendix EU(J) to the Jersey Immigration Rules, Appendix EU to the Immigration (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Rules 2008 or Appendix EU to the Isle of Man Immigration Rules together with a Positive Verification Notice from the Home Office Employer Checking Service.

4. An Application Registration Card issued by the Home Office stating that the holder is permitted to take the employment in question, together with a Positive Verification Notice from the Home Office Employer Checking Service.

5. A Positive Verification Notice issued by the Home Office Employer Checking Service to the employer or prospective employer, which indicates that the named individual may stay in the UK and is permitted to do the work in question.

Step 2 - Check

Employers must check that the documents are genuine, have not been tampered with and belong to the individual presenting them. They must also check that the individual is permitted to do the work in question.

1. Are photographs consistent across documents and with the individual presenting them? This can be checked in person, by live video link or digitally using facial recognition technology. Where facial recognition technology is used, a registered RtW DVSP must be used and the employer must obtain its comparison verifying the match between the facial image from the document and the individual.

2. Are dates of birth correct and consistent across documents?

3. Are expiry dates for time-limited permission to be in the UK in the future i.e. they have not passed (if applicable)?

4. Have work restrictions been checked to confirm the individual is permitted to do the work offered? (For students with limited permission to work during term time, employers must obtain, copy and retain details of their academic term and vacation times covering the duration of their period of study in the UK for which they will be employed).

5. Have all reasonable steps been taken to check that the documents are genuine, have not been tampered with and belong to the holder?

6. Have the reasons for any different names across documents (e.g. marriage certificate, divorce decree, deed poll) been checked? (Supporting documents should also be photocopied and a copy retained).

7. Was the check conducted with the holder present, either in person or by live video link? (If by video link, were the original documents in the employer’s physical possession?).

Step 3 – Copy

Employers must:

Make a clear copy of each document in a format that cannot be manually altered for example, as a PDF, HTML or hardcopy. Where facial recognition technology is used, employers must also obtain the comparison provided by the RtW DVSP.

If the document is a passport, copy any page containing the expiry date, nationality, DOB, signature, immigration permission, biometric details, photograph and any page containing information showing the holder’s entitlement to enter or remain in the UK and undertake the work in question. The front cover does not need to be copied.

Step 4 – Record and retain

Employers must:

Retain a secure record of the date on which the right to check was conducted, either by stating “The date on which this right to work check was made: [insert date]’ on the copy or by keeping a separate manual or digital record. Simply writing a date on the copy document on its own will not be sufficient.

Ensure all copies of documents are kept securely for the duration of employment and for 2 years afterwards, then securely destroy them.

Retain a secure copy of the comparison provided by the RtW DVSP alongside a copy of the document checked, where facial recognition technology has been used.

2. Home Office online right to work check

Step 1: Use the online service

Where an individual has an eVisa, employers must use the Home Office online right to work checking service to establish a statutory excuse by accessing the individual’s right to work information using a share code.

Employers must:

Access the Home Office right to work checking service (www.gov.uk/view-right-to-work)

Enter the individual’s share code and date of birth

Employers should also:

Enter the employer or business name correctly and in full

passages.quote:
this section to confirm that the individual carrying out the work or services is the same individual on whom a right to work check has been conducted.

Organisations should refer to the ‘Employer’s guide to right to work checks’ for further detail.

Proportionate systems and processes are in place to ensure that the person carrying out the work or services is the person on whom a right to work check was conducted.

Identity verification arrangements operate effectively in practice.

Where another party’s systems or processes are relied upon, reasonable steps are taken to ensure that the requirements are being met and those systems or processes are effective.

A clipped passport is a cancelled document (identified by the corners of certain pages in the passport being cut/removed) and therefore is not acceptable proof of right to work. ↩ ↩2

‘Definition includes those with a document which shows that the holder is entitled to readmission to the UK (RUK endorsement)’ and ILR endorsements from a Crown Dependency. ↩

Definition includes a birth certificate issued by a UK diplomatic mission (British Embassy or British High Commission) and consular birth certificates. ↩

This includes a current passport endorsed with a stamp showing an individual has been granted leave to enter and there are no work-related conditions attached. If, under the conditions of the individual’s leave, work was restricted or prohibited the endorsement placed in the individual’s passport would explicitly set that out as a condition. ↩
